note: PR #102: a full-document staleness audit (six section auditors plus a bug-verifier, in parallel) of IDEAS.md against the current tree, prompted by the file gaining a real audience. Bench tables recomputed exact; the §6 log's dated history held. 8 stale claims surfaced; 7 corrected, the 8th left as history.

decisions.question: When a documented claim has gone stale, correct it or delete it?
decisions.commitment: Correct beside the record: strike the stale trailer through, add the correction with file:line evidence. Retagged §6.11 partly->shipped (reopen_when now travels, REJECTION_FIELDS/BUNDLE_VERSION=2), §2.4 open->shipped (the 'noise' reading was overturned by a second measurement), §6.107 open->'shipped, one follow-up open'; fixed §1.4 (ed25519 landed), §2.3 (index renamed, now partial), and two §7.3 errors I had introduced this session (decision 0083->0099, and a rubric-count progression). The line-number drift inside the dated 2026-08-06 memo was left untouched.
decisions.why: Corrections land beside the record, never on top of it — a log that overwrites its own mistakes can confirm the current answer but cannot be used to check whether the reasoning was sound. Rewriting a dated memo would destroy exactly that.

decisions.question: In a 6,400-line chronological log, how do you tell a stale claim from correctly-framed history?
decisions.commitment: Only forward-looking status tags (fix open, partly) and present-tense surface claims can go stale; a dated 'measured' finding recording what was true then is history and stays. Counts pinned to run-dates (fork numbers, corpus rows, the '979 tests' figure) were left alone; a fact presented as still-true current state was verified.
decisions.why: §6 is a log. Treating its history as staleness would rewrite the record the log exists to be. The gate is the tree, not the age of the prose — a claim is stale only when it disagrees with what the code says now.
